profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Worst-speedup AND highest-latency workload (0.153x, 1.715 ms); dominates the geo_mean and is the case the parent's H1/H2/H3 hypotheses target.
Small-shape control in the same regime (dim=-1, contiguous, inner=1) to separate per-element device cost from host/launch overhead (H4) and to test whether cost scales with N or with element count.

Boundary workload of a distinct regime: dim=0 makes inner=128, so every lane is strided by 128 and only 128 programs exist. Chosen to test whether the scalar-bound finding generalises beyond contiguous last-dim scans.

findings.label: timing-1 device kernel is 98.5% Scalar-busy with 0.6% Vector: the whole body executes as scalar code, so no log-step whole-block vector scan is realised

evidence.unit: cycles; 26.5 cycles per output element over 1024x4095 elements
1711.3 us over 1024 blocks (1 program per row, BLOCK=4096)

findings.inference: H1 is supported at the level metrics can prove: a 12-step log2(4096) whole-block vector scan over 4.19M elements could not consume 1684 us of Scalar issue time. The kernel behaves as a per-lane scalar loop at ~26.5 cycles per element. Direct instruction-level confirmation (log-step shifted adds vs per-element serial loop) was requested but the server cancelled the instruction collection (RUN_CANCELLED during profile), so the exact lowering form and its instruction count remain unproven. What is proven is that whatever tl.cumsum(t, axis=0) lowers to here is not cheap and is not vector work.

findings.label: Per-element device cost is a near-constant ~26-28 cycles regardless of scan length, i.e. the cost is per element issued, not per byte moved
findings.inference: Both scales sit at the same per-element cost even though timing-0 has 4x shorter scan axes and 8x fewer programs, which rules out wave count and scan length as the dominant term and points at a fixed per-lane scalar cost (address math plus per-lane load/store). Separately, the eval latencies for timing-1/4/7 are 1.7151/1.7145/1.7101 ms for fp16/bf16/fp32, i.e. unchanged although fp32 moves twice the bytes, which independently rejects byte-proportional limits and supports per-element issue cost. Cross-dtype comparison comes from get_profile_context latency, not from this artifact.

findings.label: MTE2 is busy only 0.6% of the kernel window: there is no bulk DMA path, so H3 (transfer-bound) is rejected

evidence.unit: GB/s (2 reads + 1 write of 1024x4095 fp16 = ~25.2 MB over 1711 us)

findings.inference: The kernel moves ~25 MB of logical traffic in 1.71 ms, an effective rate of only ~15 GB/s, while the MTE2 pipe is idle 99.4% of the time. If the two masked block loads (a from k*inner, b from (k+1)*inner) were lowered to a contiguous DMA they would show up as MTE2 busy time; they do not. So the data is not arriving by bulk DMA and the workload is not limited by bandwidth or DMA granularity. Caveat: msprof pipe ratios are marginal busy-time fractions of the same window and must not be added into a time decomposition; the safe reading is only that MTE2/MTE3 are nearly idle.

findings.inference: H4 is rejected for the 4096-length case (1.71 ms device against 1.715 ms call) and for the strided dim=0 case, but holds for the small [128,1024] call where 38.6% of measured time is host-side. The execution trace shows exactly one device task per call, so the small-shape gap is launch/alloc/Python, not extra kernels. The 43.4 us figure is a difference between two independent collections (device busy time vs full-call walltime) and is not a proven per-function host breakdown.

findings.label: dim=0 (inner=128) is a separate, mixed regime: 41% Vector and 16% MTE2 busy at 68 cycles per element, so the scalar finding must not be generalised to it

evidence.unit: fractions of the 169.67 us AIV window
cycles per element (8958431 cycles / 130944 elements), vs 26.5 contiguous

findings.inference: With inner=128 the same element count costs ~2.6x more cycles and the pipeline mix is completely different (vector and MTE2 active). That is consistent with a per-lane strided gather path rather than the contiguous scalar path, i.e. this regime is bounded by access pattern as well as scalar issue. Any fix designed for inner=1 must leave this path intact and be validated separately.

performance_interpretation: For the dominating workloads the candidate is a scalar-execution-bound kernel, not a bandwidth- or launch-bound one. timing-1 spends 1684 us of its 1710 us AIV window in the Scalar pipe, ~26.5 cycles per output element, with the Vector pipe and the MTE2/MTE3 DMA pipes each under 1%. The same per-element cost appears at [128,1024] (27.9 cycles/element), so the defect is not the number of programs or the wave count; and it is unchanged between fp16, bf16 and fp32 at [1024,4096] (1.7151 / 1.7145 / 1.7101 ms), so it is not bytes. Because MTE2 is essentially idle while ~16.8 MB of input is read, the block loads in the source are evidently not being issued as bulk DMA either. The practical reading for the parent's decision: the scan is NOT already log-step and cheap. Either the whole body (address math from the runtime inner, the two masked lane-indexed loads, and the axis-0 scan) is scalarised, or the scan alone is; metrics cannot separate those two, because the direct instruction listing was cancelled by the server during collection. UB pressure (H2) is not supported but is also not measurable from this report: the report exposes no UB or spill counter, and the identical per-element cost at BLOCK=1024 (four 1024-wide FP32 live blocks = 16 KB) and BLOCK=4096 (64 KB) shows no capacity cliff between those two footprints. On the host side, only the small case carries meaningful non-device cost (~43.4 us of 112.8 us); the 4096-length case is 99.8% device. Against the reference, timing-1 is 1711 us vs 262 us for the whole six-launch PyTorch chain, so this single fused kernel is 6.5x slower than the entire reference chain it replaces.

next_experiment.action_description: Restructure only the contiguous last-dim case (inner == 1, which is exactly dim=-1 on a contiguous input: timing-0/1/3/4/6/7) into a 2D row-block kernel. One program handles BLOCK_M rows x BLOCK_N scan elements: build the address as an affine 2D tile with a compile-time-known row stride (N, and inner removed from the address expression or made constexpr), load a/b as 2D tiles whose only masks are the scan-axis tail and the row tail, keep the existing promote-to-FP32 and tl.cumsum(t, axis=1) unchanged, and store the 2D tile. Keep the current 1D kernel unchanged as the general fallback for inner != 1. Pick BLOCK_M from the actual compiled UB requirement, starting small (e.g. 4 rows at BLOCK_N=4096) rather than assuming a wide tile fits.
next_experiment.expected_impact: This attacks both scalar suspects at once by construction: an affine contiguous 2D tile gives the backend a bulk MTE2 load instead of per-lane masked loads, and the row dimension amortises any residual serial step of the scan over BLOCK_M elements. Predicted counter changes on timing-1 at the same source SHA: aiv_mte2_ratio rises from 0.006 to clearly non-trivial, aiv_vec_ratio rises from 0.006, aiv_scalar_ratio falls from 0.985, and aiv_total_cycles per element falls from ~26.5 to single digits. Target device time for timing-1 well under 300 us (reference is 262 us for the whole six-launch chain), which would move timing-1/4/7 from ~0.15-0.19x toward parity and lift the headline geo_mean above 0.3535.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: UB capacity is the main risk and this project has already hit it (SELU needed 288 KiB against a 192 KiB limit): four live FP32 row-blocks of BLOCK_N=4096 cost 4 x BLOCK_M x 4096 x 4 bytes, so verify the compiled UB figure instead of extrapolating from an fp16 tile. If the 2D tile cannot fit, do not shrink BLOCK_N into a carry chain inside this experiment; propose the chunked scan with a serial carry as a separate, explicitly sequenced change. Numerics: keep the existing FP32 promotion, scan order and dx handling byte-for-byte; do not change accumulation dtype here, because earlier device probes showed FP16 increment scanned in FP32 does not match the reference on long sequences, and the timing inputs are a separate hard gate from the 24 correctness cases. Rollback: the current kernel stays in the file as the inner != 1 branch, so reverting the fast path costs one branch. Falsification: if a re-profile of the new source shows Scalar still at ~26 cycles/element with MTE2 and Vector still ~0, the tile/pointer hypothesis is dead and the next step becomes a manual log-step shifted-add scan over an already-2D tile (option b), not more tile sweeping.
success_criteria: All 24 correctness workloads still PASS on the same contract and tolerance
All 9 timing inputs pass numeric validation a second time; the timing phase is a separate gate and passing the 24 correctness cases does not cover it
Headline geo_mean above the 0.3535 baseline, with the [1024,4096] cases (timing-1/4/7) clearly above their baseline 0.15/0.19/0.19 speedups

On a re-profile of the new source SHA for timing-1: aiv_scalar_ratio falls from 0.985 and aiv_mte2_ratio and aiv_vec_ratio rise above roughly 0.05, i.e. the predicted counter movement actually happens together with the latency drop
timing-2/5/8 (dim=0, inner=128) show no regression; they are a different regime and must keep their current behaviour

msprof pipeline ratios are marginal busy-time fractions of the same AIV window and overlap in time; they are used here only to reject pipes that are near-idle, never added into a time decomposition or a Roofline.
msprof device durations are diagnostic and do not replace eval latency; all speedup, candidate latency and reference latency values in this analysis come from get_profile_context.
The ~43.4 us small-shape gap is a difference between a device busy-time collection and a full-call walltime collection, not a measured per-function host breakdown.
open_questions: Is the ~26.5 cycles/element produced by the axis-0 scan lowering, by the per-lane masked loads, or by the scalar address math from the runtime inner? Metrics cannot separate them; the cancelled instruction listing would have.

H2 (UB pressure/spill) is neither supported nor excluded: msprof exposes no UB-occupancy or spill counter, and the equal per-element cost at 16 KB (BLOCK=1024) and 64 KB (BLOCK=4096) of live FP32 block data shows no cliff between those two footprints.

Does the reference path for the dim=0 bf16 case (timing-5, the only workload above 1x at 1.247x) include a slow vendor scan rather than a genuinely better kernel? The candidate latency there is 0.241 ms for both fp16 and bf16, so the >1x result comes from the 0.301 ms reference, not from a candidate improvement.
What share of the small-shape host cost is Triton argument marshalling versus torch.empty allocation for the output? The gap is bounded but not decomposed.
